sources: PRIMARY: IMO conventions page - the treaty process. Adoption is by the relevant IMO organ or by a diplomatic conference. A State may express consent by signature alone where the treaty so provides; most multilateral treaties instead allow signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, where signature does not bind and the State must subsequently deposit a formal instrument with the depositary. It cites Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Article 14(2): 'the consent of a State to be bound by a treaty is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification'. PRIMARY: IMO conventions page - entry into force and amendment. A convention becomes binding only after governments formally accept it. Early conventions typically required acceptance by two-thirds of contracting States, which sometimes meant more acceptances were needed for entry into force than for amendments, causing delay. Conventions of an important technical nature generally set higher requirements involving both a number of States and a percentage of world merchant fleet gross tonnage. The tacit acceptance procedure was devised to accelerate amendment: an amendment is deemed to have been accepted unless objections are received before a deadline. blocks.h: 1. Adoption is not entry into force

blocks.p: A convention is adopted either by the competent IMO organ - Assembly, MSC, MEPC or Legal Committee - or by a diplomatic conference. Adoption settles the text and does no more: it binds no State, and an adopted convention may never enter into force at all. The text is then opened for signature and deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary.

blocks.h: 2. How a State expresses consent to be bound

blocks.p: Between adoption and entry into force sits the step that matters: each State must express its consent to be bound, by one of three routes -

ul: signature alone, where the treaty so provides or the negotiating States so agreed;
signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, the normal course for multilateral conventions;
accession, where the State did not sign within the signature period.

blocks.p: In the second and third cases the State is bound only on depositing a formal instrument with the depositary, who records it, counts it towards the entry into force condition and notifies all other States.

blocks.h: 3. The two terms the question names

blocks.p: (ii) Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. The State signs, but signature does not bind it; it indicates an intention to proceed. The State becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification. Its modern purpose is to give the State time to enact domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements before committing internationally. Acceptance and approval are the same act under less formal names, used where a constitution does not demand the fuller procedure: VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.

(i) Accession. The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign - because the signature period closed, or it was not a negotiating State. It is a single step: no prior signature, simply deposit of an instrument of accession, permitted by VCLT Article 15 where the treaty so provides. Once deposited it has exactly the same legal effect as ratification. The difference is the route, not the destination.

blocks.h: 4. The entry into force provision, and why it matters

blocks.p: Every convention contains a final clause fixing entry into force, normally a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. Its importance is fourfold:

ul: it prevents an instrument binding a handful of States while the rest operate to another standard, which would distort competition;
it fixes a certain date from which obligations, surveys and certificates run, so Administrations, ROs, owners and yards work to one deadline;
it provides the interval for flag States to legislate, class to develop rules and industry to build or retrofit;
it gives legitimacy - a convention in force across most world tonnage is enforceable through port State control against the remainder, which is what makes no more favourable treatment work.

blocks.h: 5. Conventions of an important technical nature

blocks.p: For a convention of important technical nature - one dictating construction, equipment or operation - States observe a stiffer double condition: a number of States and a percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. A count of States alone could be met by many small flags while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving the convention in force on paper and irrelevant at sea.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, requiring not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; in force 25 May 1980.
The 1978 MARPOL Protocol - in force twelve months after not less than fifteen States constituting not less than fifty per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage had become Parties.

blocks.p: Older conventions typically required two-thirds of contracting States, which occasionally meant more acceptances were needed to bring an instrument into force than to amend it.

blocks.h: 6. Keeping the convention current once in force

blocks.p: A technical convention is worthless if it cannot keep pace, and explicit acceptance failed on that point: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances and none entered into force.

IMO's answer was the tacit acceptance procedure, used in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL and the collision regulations. It reverses the default: an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication to Contracting Governments, unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Amendments now enter into force typically within 18 to 24 months. Once in force internationally each flag State must still give the instrument effect domestically - in India through the Merchant Shipping Act and rules made under it - and it is that domestic instrument which is enforced against the ship.

The stem prints no limbs but makes four separate demands, and the commonest failure is to answer the first and drift. Following one instrument through its life from adoption to amendment answers all four in a single narrative, and putting the two named terms side by side in step 3 lets the contrast be drawn explicitly - which is what an explain the terms instruction is asking for.

blocks.h: Why the machinery looks so cumbersome

blocks.p: A treaty binds sovereign States, and no State can be bound without its own consent - that single constitutional fact generates the whole apparatus. Adoption cannot bind, because the conference does not speak for any government. Signature cannot ordinarily bind, because most constitutions require a legislature to act before the executive can commit. Hence the two-step route, the deposited instrument, the depositary who counts, and the threshold that has to be reached before anyone is obliged to do anything. Tacit acceptance is the one place where the system bends: consent is still required, but silence is treated as consent, and that inversion is what made a technical convention maintainable.

blocks.h: Why this matters to a Chief Engineer

blocks.p: It explains a situation seen constantly in practice: an amendment has been adopted, the industry press is full of it, class has issued guidance - and it does not yet apply to the ship. It also explains why a ship may be subject to a requirement her flag State has not ratified, through port State control and the no more favourable treatment principle, and why the certificate on the bulkhead is issued under national law rather than under the convention directly. The IMO Net-Zero Framework - the draft new MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 5, which was approved but not adopted when the extraordinary MEPC session adjourned in October 2025 - is a live illustration of an instrument stalled between approval and adoption. It is examined directly in QP2602 Q8.

blocks.h: Four words that are not synonyms

ul: Adoption - the text is settled. Nobody is bound.
Signature - intent indicated. Ordinarily still nobody is bound.
Ratification / acceptance / approval - a signatory State becomes bound on deposit. The three differ in domestic formality only.
Accession - a non-signatory State becomes bound on deposit, in one step.

blocks.p: And separately: entry into force of the convention is not entry into force for a particular State, which usually follows some months after that State deposits its own instrument.

ul: Saying a convention is in force once adopted, or once signed.
Using ratification and accession as synonyms, or inventing a difference between ratification, acceptance and approval.
Giving only a number of States for a technical convention and omitting the tonnage percentage - the double condition is the point of that part of the question.
Describing tacit acceptance as the way a convention enters into force. It is the way an amendment does.
Forgetting that the flag State must still legislate domestically.
Confusing a reservation with a declaration, or asserting that reservations are freely available - many technical conventions restrict them.
'State the provision and its importance' - two things. Most candidates state the provision and never say why it exists.
'For a convention of important technical nature' is a specific category, and the expected answer is the double condition with a real example. A general answer scores poorly here.
The two terms are printed as (i) and (ii) with no marks attached, which tempts candidates to treat them as an afterthought. They are a named, explicit demand and should be answered properly.

Your flag State has not ratified a convention. Can a port State detain you under it?

blocks.p: One instrument, six stages: ADOPT, CONSENT, TERMS, THRESHOLD, TONNAGE, AMEND. Two pairs of numbers carry the technical-convention part: SOLAS 25 and 50%, MARPOL 15 and 50%. One pair carries amendment: two years, one-third or 50%. And one sentence carries the distinction the question asks for: ratification is the second step for a State that signed; accession is the only step for a State that did not.

ul: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 - Art 14(2) acceptance and approval; Art 15 accession.
SOLAS 1974 - final clauses on entry into force; Article VIII amendments and tacit acceptance.
MARPOL 73/78 - Article 15 and the 1978 Protocol's entry into force condition.
IMO Convention Article 38(e) - the functions under which committees act.
India - the Merchant Shipping Act and rules made under it as the domestic vehicle.

blocks.p: MIW holds no licensed copy of SOLAS or MARPOL. The entry into force conditions and the tacit acceptance thresholds are cited from the IMO's own explanatory material - which quotes the SOLAS wording directly - and from convention summaries, rather than from the convention texts. Entry into force provisions are named by effect where the article number could not be confirmed, in preference to asserting a number that might be wrong. The Vienna Convention Articles 14(2) and 15 are likewise cited as quoted on the IMO's page rather than read in the Convention. None of this material is time-sensitive: the machinery has been stable for decades and the two worked examples are historical facts.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Adoption is not entry into force. An IMO organ or a diplomatic conference adopts the text; that settles the wording and binds nobody. The text is then opened for signature and a State expresses consent to be bound in one of three ways: signature alone where the treaty allows it; signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, where signature is only an indication of intent and the State must later deposit a formal instrument - the interval being what lets it enact domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements, with acceptance and approval being less formal equivalents of ratification under VCLT Article 14(2); and accession, a single step by which a State that did not sign within the signature period becomes a party by depositing an instrument of accession, under VCLT Article 15. quick_revision.major_trap: Treating adoption, signature and entry into force as one event, or using ratification and accession as synonyms. Signature subject to ratification is a two-step route for a State that was present and signed; accession is a one-step route for a State that was not, or that did not sign in time. The effect once the instrument is deposited is the same - the difference is the path, not the result. The second trap is conflating the entry into force of the convention with the entry into force of an amendment: they use different thresholds and different procedures.

The second generation intact stability criteria remain INTERIM guidelines at the sitting date and are not a mandatory SOLAS requirement. Whether and when they become mandatory was not established and the answer does not assert it.

The phrase 'roll design assessment software' is not an IMO term of art. The answer treats it as the direct stability assessment and onboard decision-support tooling that the second generation criteria contemplate, and says so rather than assuming a single named product.

blocks.p: The forces a lashing system must hold - racking of the container frame, tipping, tension in lashing rods, shear and tension in twistlocks - are driven overwhelmingly by transverse acceleration, which rises with both roll angle and roll acceleration. A stack safe at 15 degrees can exceed its permissible racking load well before 30. Roll is therefore the governing design case, and keeping the ship out of excessive roll is itself a securing measure.

blocks.h: 2. The dynamic failure modes the software assesses

ul: Parametric rolling - the container-ship problem. Large bow flare and a wide flat stern make the waterplane, and therefore GM, vary substantially between wave crest and trough. In head or following seas, when the roll period is roughly twice the wave encounter period, that periodic stiffness variation pumps energy into roll and large angles build in a few cycles, with no beam sea to warn of it.
Synchronous rolling - roll period close to the encounter period in beam or quartering seas.
Excessive acceleration - a stiff ship with high GM and heavy containers stowed high has a short roll period and severe lateral accelerations even at modest angles.
Pure loss of stability, and surf-riding and broaching in following seas.
These five are the failure modes of the Second Generation Intact Stability Criteria (MSC.1/Circ.1627), which at this date are interim guidelines, not a mandatory SOLAS requirement.

blocks.h: 3. What the software does with them

blocks.p: The criteria apply in three levels: levels 1 and 2 screen a design by empirical formulae and simplified models, and level 3, direct stability assessment, simulates the ship in irregular waves in the time domain across the range of loading conditions, headings, speeds and sea states. The output is not a pass mark but two practical products: operational limitations - a restricted GM range, a limiting sea state, stowage constraints written into the loading manual - and operational guidance, typically a polar diagram of speed against relative heading marking the combinations to avoid.

blocks.h: 4. How it is used on board

ul: The loading and lashing computer calculates the accelerations for the actual planned condition and checks the resulting forces against the permissible values in the Cargo Securing Manual before the stow is fixed. Stack weight, stack height and GM are adjusted until the lashing forces come within limits.
Decision-support software presents the operational guidance in service, so the master can alter speed or heading to move out of a dangerous combination - the classic remedy in MSC.1/Circ.1228.

The calculation is only as good as its inputs. Under SOLAS chapter VI regulation 2 the shipper must declare the verified gross mass of a packed container; a misdeclared weight corrupts both the GM and the stack-load check.

blocks.h: 5. Status, purpose and approval of the CSM

blocks.p: Under SOLAS chapter VI regulation 5 and chapter VII regulation 5, cargo units and cargo transport units must be loaded, stowed and secured throughout the voyage in accordance with a Cargo Securing Manual approved by the Administration - in practice by a recognized organization on its behalf. It is ship-specific and a mandatory carriage document, not guidance, and is laid out to the standard structure of MSC.1/Circ.1353/Rev.2.

ul: General - purpose, definitions and application.

Securing devices and arrangements - an inventory and specification of the fixed fittings (lashing eyes, deck sockets, container foundations) with their locations and maximum securing load, and of the portable devices (twistlocks, lashing rods, turnbuckles, bridge fittings), with their strength, inspection, maintenance and replacement criteria.

Stowage and securing of containers and other standardised cargo - the approved lashing patterns, permissible stack weights and heights, permissible racking and corner-post loads, and the forces assumed to act.
Stowage and securing of non-standardised and semi-standardised cargo, with handling and safety instructions.
Annexes, including the procedure for evaluating the efficiency of securing arrangements for semi- and non-standardised cargo, harmonised with Annex 13 of the CSS Code.
For container ships, the Cargo Safe Access Plan - the safe routes, working platforms, lashing positions, fencing and lighting for the people doing the lashing.
SOLAS VI/5 and VII/5 - the requirement for the approved manual; SOLAS VI/2 - cargo information and verified gross mass.

blocks.p: Two printed limbs, so two visible halves. Limb (i) is the one candidates fumble, because 'roll design assessment software' is not an IMO term and there is a temptation to write generally about rolling. Anchor it instead on a named framework - the five failure modes and three assessment levels of MSC.1/Circ.1627 - and on what the output is actually for: operational limitations and a speed/heading diagram. Limb (ii) asks three things - use, content, and associated regulations - and the third is a list the examiner can tick, so never let it be squeezed.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb (i) coherent

blocks.p: Securing and stability are usually taught as separate subjects, and the question is really asking you to join them. The lashing gear has a fixed strength; the sea does not negotiate. The only variables the ship controls are how much roll it experiences and how the weight is distributed. So the software is not an academic seakeeping exercise - it is the thing that tells you which GM range, which stack weights and which speed and heading combinations keep the accelerations inside what the lashings can already hold. Parametric roll is the sharpest case because it happens in head and following seas, where a watchkeeper is least expecting a roll problem.

blocks.h: Why parametric roll is a container-ship problem specifically

blocks.p: It is a hull-form consequence. Container ships have pronounced bow flare and a wide, flat transom to maximise deck stowage. When a wave crest is amidships the waterplane at the ends is narrower than in still water and stability falls; when the crest is at the ends the waterplane widens and stability rises. Encounter that variation at about twice the roll period and you are pumping the roll at its own resonance - the same physics as a child pumping a swing by shifting weight twice per cycle. Bulk carriers and tankers, with fuller and more prismatic ends, vary far less and are much less prone to it.

ul: Describing the second generation criteria as a mandatory SOLAS requirement. At this sitting they are interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1627. Say so - the qualification is worth more than the claim.
Treating the CSM as guidance or as a company document. It is approved by the Administration and required by SOLAS; carrying an unapproved or non-ship-specific manual is a detainable deficiency.
Listing lashing gear but omitting the maximum securing load and the permissible stack weight and height - those are the numbers the manual exists to provide.
Forgetting the people. Annex 14 and the Cargo Safe Access Plan are about the lashing gang's safe access, not about the cargo, and a full answer says so.
Confusing the CSS Code (stowage and securing) with the CSC 1972 (the container's own structural approval). They answer different questions - is the box secured, versus is the box fit to be stacked.

blocks.p:
"You are in head seas. Can you have a rolling problem?" Yes - that is precisely parametric rolling, and answering "no, rolling needs beam seas" is the trap the question is built around.

"Your GM is high. Is that good for container securing?" No. A stiff ship has a short roll period and higher accelerations; excessive acceleration is one of the five failure modes. More GM is not more safety for a container stow.

"Does every container ship need a Cargo Safe Access Plan?" Be precise. The full Annex 14 applies to ships keel-laid on or after 1 January 2015; for older ships only the training and familiarization, introduction, maintenance and specialized design sections apply. A flat 'all container ships must have one' overstates it.

"What did the shipper have to do with your lashing calculation?" Declare the verified gross mass under SOLAS VI/2. A misdeclared box corrupts the whole calculation.

ul: Who approves the Cargo Securing Manual? The Administration, or a recognized organization acting for it.
Which SOLAS regulations require it? Chapter VI regulation 5 and chapter VII regulation 5.
What is Annex 13 of the CSS Code for? Assessing the efficiency of securing arrangements for semi-standardised and non-standardised cargo - the cargo the standard lashing patterns do not cover.
Name the five second generation stability failure modes. Parametric roll, pure loss of stability, excessive acceleration, dead ship condition, surf-riding and broaching.
What is the immediate action if parametric rolling develops? Change speed or heading to break the resonance, per MSC.1/Circ.1228.
What is maximum securing load? The permissible working load of a securing device, given in the CSM against each fitting.

blocks.p: MOTION - MANUAL. Limb (i) is motion: why roll rules (1), the failure modes (2), what the software computes (3), how it is used on board (4). Limb (ii) is the manual: status (5), content (6), the codes behind it (7). Within limb (ii), remember content as WHAT - WHERE - HOW MUCH - WHO: what gear is fitted, where it is, how much load it may take, and who has to walk out there safely.

questions.understand_first: A lashing has a fixed strength and the sea does not negotiate, so the only things the ship controls are how much it rolls and how the weight is stacked. That is why a stability tool answers a cargo-securing question: the software's job is to find the loading conditions, speeds and headings in which acceleration would exceed what the gear can already hold, and then fence them off - as a GM range and stack limits at the design stage, and as a speed-and-heading diagram in service. The sting is that the worst container-ship case, parametric rolling, happens in head and following seas, where a watchkeeper is least expecting to have a roll problem at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the CSS Code from the CSC 1972.
retrieval_cards.answer: The CSS Code governs how cargo is stowed and secured on the ship. The CSC 1972 governs the container itself - its structural approval, the safety approval plate and the examination scheme that keeps it fit to be stacked and lashed.

blocks.h: 1. Why war risk is a separate cover

blocks.p: War perils are not uninsurable. Under section 2(e) of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, "maritime perils" expressly include war perils, captures, seizures, restraints and detainments of princes and peoples. What removes them from the ordinary policy is the policy wording, not the statute: the standard hull and cargo forms carry a war exclusion - historically the free of capture and seizure clause. The cover is then bought back separately, on different terms, by a different market, at a separately negotiated price. That deletion-and-buy-back is the whole architecture of war risk cover.

ul: Hull war risks - written on the Institute War and Strikes Clauses (Hulls-Time) by specialist war underwriters or by a war risks mutual association, covering physical loss of or damage to the ship.

P&I war risks - the Clubs exclude war risks under their Rules. In their place the International Group provides a separate excess war risks P&I cover, sitting above the ship's hull war policy or proper value, up to a fixed limit and cancellable at short notice. It answers third-party liabilities: crew death and injury, pollution, wreck removal, collision liability.
Cargo war risks - the Institute War Clauses (Cargo), attaching while the goods are waterborne.
Extensions bought alongside: war loss of hire, crew war bonus and kidnap and ransom.
War, civil war, revolution, rebellion, insurrection and civil strife arising from them, and any hostile act by or against a belligerent power.
Capture, seizure, arrest, restraint or detainment, and the consequences of any attempt at them.
Derelict weapons of war - mines, torpedoes and bombs.
Strikes, riots and civil commotions, and labour disturbances, in the combined War and Strikes forms.
Terrorism, and persons acting maliciously or from a political motive, including sabotage.
Confiscation or expropriation by a government or authority.

Blocking and trapping: where the ship is detained or prevented from free movement for a stated continuous period, the assured may treat her as a constructive total loss without proving physical damage. This is the aspect most specific to a Gulf scenario and the one candidates most often miss.
Hostile detonation of a nuclear weapon.
Outbreak of war between the major powers - the "five powers" provision, on which cover terminates automatically.
Requisition or pre-emption by the ship's own flag State.
Ordinary judicial process, arrest for debt, and financial default.
Cyber loss under the market cyber exclusion, and any loss whose payment would breach a sanctions regime.

blocks.h: 5. Containing the exposure - area, notice and price

ul: Listed Areas. The London market's Joint War Committee publishes areas of perceived enhanced risk for hull war, strikes, terrorism and related perils, assessed against a risk benchmark by an independent consultant. The list is the trigger for everything that follows.

Notification and additional premium. Entering a Listed Area requires prior notice to underwriters; the annual cover is in effect suspended for that transit and reinstated only against a separately negotiated additional war risk premium, priced per transit and per vessel and moving with the threat.
Trading warranties. The policy warrants that the ship will not enter specified areas without consent. Entering without notice is a breach and prejudices the cover.

Short cancellation. War cover is not an annual promise. It is cancellable on seven days' notice under London market wordings - and on forty-eight hours under some United States wordings - and terminates automatically on the great-power and nuclear triggers. This is the single most powerful protection the underwriter holds.

blocks.h: 6. Limits, conditions and the Club position

ul: Limits and deductibles - per vessel, per event and in the aggregate, so a single incident cannot be open-ended.
Conditions of cover - routeing and transit windows, restricted port stays, convoy or naval escort participation, hardening and watchkeeping measures, and armed guards where lawfully permitted.

Reinsurance. Underwriters retrocede war exposure to a specialist market; the International Group's own reinsurance programme treats war separately, which is precisely why the Clubs write it as a distinct excess cover rather than inside the pooled entry.
Sanctions and due diligence - screening of trades, counterparties and ownership, with a sanctions clause allowing cover to be withheld.
Underwriting discipline - continuous monitoring, shorter policy periods, declining or re-rating vessels in particular trades, and Club circulars warning members before a situation deteriorates.

blocks.p: The two printed limbs are unequal in difficulty. Limb (a) is knowledge - what the cover is and what is in it - and most candidates can fill it. Limb (b) is where the marks are actually won, because it asks about the underwriter's position rather than the shipowner's, and most candidates have never been asked to think from that side. Give limb (b) genuine weight: Listed Areas, additional premium, warranties, seven days' notice, limits, reinsurance, sanctions. Open on the statutory point - war perils are maritime perils under the Act - because it frames everything that follows and takes one sentence.

Almost every marine cover question is about what a policy includes. War risk is the opposite: the ordinary policy deletes the peril and a second contract writes it back. That is why there are two underwriters, two premiums, two sets of conditions and two cancellation regimes on one ship. Once that is clear, the P&I structure follows without memorising: the Club excludes war under its Rules, so the war P&I cover has to sit outside the pool as a separate excess layer - and being outside the pool is exactly why it carries a fixed limit and a short cancellation notice, which ordinary Club cover does not.

blocks.h: Why the underwriter's protections look the way they do

blocks.p: War risk is uninsurable in the actuarial sense: the losses are correlated. An ordinary hull book relies on the fact that one ship's grounding tells you nothing about the next ship's. In a war zone every insured vessel is exposed to the same event on the same day, so the law of large numbers stops working. Every protection in limb (b) is a response to that single problem - the Listed Area identifies the correlated zone, the additional premium prices each entry into it, the notice period lets the underwriter exit before exposure accumulates, and the limits cap what any one event can cost. Presenting them as a list of tricks scores less than presenting them as one coherent answer to correlation.

ul: Saying war perils are uninsurable or excluded by law. They are maritime perils under section 2(e) of the Marine Insurance Act 1963; the exclusion is contractual.
Treating war cover as part of the P&I entry. The Clubs exclude it and provide a separate excess cover instead.
Omitting blocking and trapping. Detention for a stated continuous period founds a constructive total loss claim with no physical damage at all - the aspect a Gulf question is most likely aimed at.
Quoting a specific premium rate or reciting today's Listed Areas. Both move continuously; describe the mechanism instead.
Confusing piracy with war risk. Depending on the form, piracy may sit in the hull policy or in the war policy - say that it depends on the wording rather than asserting one answer.
Forgetting that war cover can be cancelled at seven days. Candidates assume an annual policy is an annual promise.

"Your ship is detained in a Gulf port for months but is undamaged. Do you have a claim?" Potentially yes - the blocking and trapping provision founds a constructive total loss once the stated continuous period is exceeded. Answering "no, there is no damage" fails the question.

"Is war risk covered by your P&I Club?" No - it is excluded by the Rules, with a separate excess war P&I cover provided instead.

"You are ordered into a Listed Area at short notice. What must you do?" Notify underwriters before entering and agree the additional premium. Entering first is a breach of a trading warranty and may prejudice the cover.

"What ends the cover instantly, whatever the premium paid?" Hostile detonation of a nuclear weapon, and outbreak of war between the major powers.

blocks.p: DELETE - BUY BACK - FENCE OFF. Delete: the ordinary policy excludes war though the Act calls it a maritime peril (step 1). blocks.p: Ship health and vector control are governed by the International Health Regulations (2005), a binding instrument of the World Health Organization, as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024. The 2024 amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025. The IHR work through designated points of entry, competent authorities at those points, and a small set of ship documents.

ul: It makes the rules. WHO adopts the IHR and prescribes the model certificates in Annex 3 and the Ship Declaration of Health in Annex 8, so the documents are the same worldwide.

It identifies where vector control is needed. Under Annex 5, WHO publishes on a regular basis a list of areas where disinsection or other vector control measures are recommended for conveyances arriving from them, through temporary or standing recommendations.

It advises methods and materials. Where WHO has advised methods for disinsection, deratting, disinfection or decontamination, those should be used unless the competent authority is satisfied that others are as safe and reliable (Article 27), and States should accept measures applied elsewhere by WHO-advised methods.

It certifies and publishes. On a State Party's request WHO may, after appropriate investigation, certify that a port meets the IHR requirements (Article 20(4)), publishes certification guidelines and the list of certified ports (20(5)), and publishes the lists of authorized ports notified by States Parties (20(3)).

It provides technical guidance - notably the WHO Handbook for inspection of ships and issuance of ship sanitation certificates - and declares Public Health Emergencies of International Concern with temporary recommendations.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - the health authority for IHR purposes, under which the National IHR Focal Point sits.

Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), and under it the Port Health Organisation, headed by the Port Health Officer - the competent authority at the point of entry. It inspects ships, baggage, cargo and containers, supervises control measures and issues the ship sanitation certificates, working under the Indian Port Health Rules, 1955 with the IHR 2005.
Directorate General of Shipping, through its Maritime Health Branch, on the seafarer side - approving medical examiners and governing seafarers' medical fitness examination and certification.
Port authorities and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways support these functions at the ports themselves.

Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate (SSCEC) - issued where the competent authority is satisfied that the ship is free of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs, so that no control measures are required (Article 39(6)).

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (SSCC) - issued where control measures were required and have been satisfactorily completed, and it records the evidence found and the measures taken (Article 39(5)). Under Annex 5 the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them are recorded on this certificate. If a satisfactory result could not be obtained, the authority notes that on the certificate (Article 39(7)).

blocks.p: Both follow the model in Annex 3, and they replaced the former Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates. Alongside them the master submits a Ship Declaration of Health under Article 37, to the model in Annex 8 - a declaration, not a certificate. Separately, and concerning the crew rather than the ship, seafarers hold medical fitness certificates under MLC 2006 and STCW.

blocks.h: 5. Issue in India, validity and extension

ul: In India they are issued by the Port Health Officer at a port authorized for the purpose and notified to WHO. Under Article 20(3) a State Party notifies which ports may issue the SSCC, which may issue the SSCEC only, and which may grant the one-month extension.
Validity: a maximum of six months, for both the SSCEC and the SSCC (Article 39(1)).
Extension: by one month, where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at that port - the extension carries the ship to a port where the certificate can be obtained.

Where no valid certificate is produced, or evidence of a public health risk is found on board, the State Party may proceed under Article 27(1) - treating the ship as affected and requiring disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Control measures are to be carried out whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading (Article 39(4)).

For Indian coastal trade calling where no Port Health Officer is available, DG Shipping has provided for a Statement of Compliance issued by an authorized medical examiner, to be endorsed at the earliest available opportunity.

blocks.p: Four separate questions are asked and each must be visibly answered - WHO's role, the national agencies, the certificates, and issue/validity/extension in India. Take them in the printed order and head each one. The final limb contains the two numbers the examiner is certainly looking for, six months and one month, so never let it be squeezed by a long essay on WHO.

blocks.h: The currency point that will separate answers

blocks.p: The IHR were amended in 2024 and those amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025 - before this paper was sat. One visible consequence: Article 37 is now the "Ship Declaration of Health". In the original 2005 text it was the "Maritime Declaration of Health", and that older name is what almost every textbook, coaching note and older syllabus still uses. Both texts were compared directly for this answer: the original uses "Maritime Declaration of Health" throughout and never the new name; the consolidated amended text uses "Ship Declaration of Health" throughout and never the old one. Using the current name, and being able to say why it changed, is a cheap and genuine mark.

blocks.h: Ship health and crew health are two different systems

blocks.p: The question asks about "the ship and the crew", and the two run on separate tracks with separate authorities. Ship health is WHO and the IHR, administered in India by the Port Health Organisation under DGHS and the Ministry of Health, and evidenced by the SSCC or SSCEC. Crew health is MLC 2006 and STCW, administered in India by DG Shipping through approved medical examiners, and evidenced by seafarers' medical fitness certificates. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates. It is not - the Port Health Officer issues those.

ul: Calling the SSCC/SSCEC a Deratting Certificate. Those were the predecessors under the earlier Regulations and were replaced under the IHR 2005 - the scope widened from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.
Saying the certificates are valid for six months extendable by six months. The extension is one month, and only where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at that port.
Confusing the SSCC with the SSCEC. Exemption means no measures were needed; Control means measures were required and were completed.
Treating the Ship Declaration of Health as a certificate. It is a declaration by the master, to the Annex 8 model, and a State may dispense with it entirely under Article 37(4).
Naming WHO as an enforcement body. WHO recommends, certifies ports on request and publishes; the competent authority at the point of entry enforces.

blocks.p:
"Your certificate expired yesterday and the port cannot inspect - what happens?" The one-month extension in Article 39(1) exists precisely for this, and under Article 20(3)(c) States notify which of their ports may grant it, so that the ship can reach a port where the certificate is obtainable.

"When should the inspection be done?" Whenever possible with the ship and holds empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading - Article 39(4). Answering "any time" misses a printed requirement.

"What does WHO actually do about mosquitoes?" It publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended for conveyances arriving from them, and advises the methods. States Parties then run vector control programmes at points of entry - to a minimum distance of 400 metres from the operational areas under Annex 5.

ul: Who issues the SSCC in India? The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO.
Under which ministry does the Port Health Organisation sit? The Directorate General of Health Services, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Validity and extension? Maximum six months; extendable by one month where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port.
What is recorded on an SSCC? The evidence found and the control measures taken - including, under Annex 5, the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them.
What happens if you cannot produce a valid certificate? The State Party may treat the ship as affected under Article 27(1) and require disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Which convention covers the crew's medical fitness rather than the ship's sanitation? MLC 2006, with STCW for certification - administered in India by DG Shipping.

blocks.p: RULE - AGENCY - PAPER - CLOCK. Rule: IHR 2005 as amended, WHO's role (steps 1 to 2). Agency: MoHFW, DGHS, Port Health Organisation and the Port Health Officer, with DG Shipping on the crew side (step 3). Paper: SSCEC, SSCC, and the Ship Declaration of Health (step 4). Clock: six months, plus one (step 5). Two numbers, two certificates, one declaration.

One protects the world from the ship - vectors, infection and contamination crossing borders in a hull - and that is WHO's International Health Regulations, enforced by a port health authority and evidenced by a ship sanitation certificate. blocks.h: 1. The framework these processes sit inside

blocks.p: A ship using LNG as fuel is designed and operated under SOLAS chapter II-1 part G and the IGF Code; the bunkering operation itself is specified by ISO 20519 - equipment, procedures, competence and documentation. Safety rests on a two-stage emergency shutdown system, with the delivery facility and the receiving ship joined by an ESD link so both act together. Before transfer, a safety zone is set, compatibility and mooring agreed, and the checklist and bunkering plan completed.

Carried out when a tank is being brought back into service after refit, repair or inerting - before any liquid is introduced. The tank is full of inert gas or nitrogen, and that atmosphere must be replaced with methane vapour.

ul: Why. Any carbon dioxide in inert gas would freeze at LNG temperature and block valves, filters and lines. Nitrogen does not freeze but is non-condensable: it accumulates in the vapour space, raises tank pressure, degrades the fuel's calorific value and upsets reliquefaction and gas supply.

How. LNG is taken from the supply through a vaporiser to produce warm methane vapour, which is admitted at the top of the tank. Being lighter than nitrogen, it forms a layer that pushes the heavier inert gas down and out through the bottom liquid line.
Where it goes. The displaced gas is led to the vent mast with attention to dispersion, or returned to the supply.

Completion. Sampling at the outlet continues until the hydrocarbon content reaches the specified value and carbon dioxide falls below its limit. The figures are set by the ship's manual and the containment system, not by a universal rule.

blocks.p: Once the tank holds methane vapour it is still warm. Cooling down brings the tank, pipework and manifold gradually towards LNG temperature, about minus 162 degrees Celsius, before bulk filling begins.

ul: Why. To avoid thermal shock and excessive thermal stress in the tank structure and insulation; and to avoid the violent flash-off that occurs when LNG meets warm surfaces, which would over-pressurise the tank and swamp the vapour handling capacity.
How. LNG is admitted in small controlled quantities through spray nozzles at the top of the tank, evaporating as it falls and cooling the structure evenly.

Rate control. The permitted rate of temperature fall is limited by the tank designer and class, and temperatures are watched at fixed sensors through the tank to keep the structure cooling uniformly rather than locally.
Completion. When the sensors reach the target and are stable, bulk transfer starts at a low initial rate and is ramped up only once pressures and temperatures are seen to be steady.

blocks.p: LNG boils continuously from heat ingress, and filling a tank displaces the vapour already in it. Vapour management is the control of tank pressure within the design limit throughout, and it is the process that actually governs how fast bunkering can proceed.

ul: Vapour return line - the primary method. A connection back to the bunker source returns the displaced vapour to its tanks, balancing pressure on both sides and removing the need to vent to atmosphere.
Consumption - burning the gas in the ship's engines, boilers or generators where the plant is running.
Reliquefaction where fitted, returning boil-off to the tank as liquid.
Gas combustion unit - burning off surplus gas safely where it cannot be used.
Controlled venting to the vent mast - a last resort only, because released methane is a potent greenhouse gas and venting is operationally and environmentally constrained.

Supporting controls. Spray filling to condense vapour; monitoring against the relief valve setting; level alarms and ESD trips; and attention to stratification and rollover where LNG of a different density is loaded onto an existing heel.

blocks.p: The emergency release system exists so that the transfer connection can be parted quickly and without spilling if the two vessels move beyond safe limits, if moorings fail, or in fire. Its heart is the emergency release coupling - a dry-break coupling with interlocked isolating valves which close before the halves separate, so the liquid held in the line is contained and the release of LNG and gas is minimised.

ul: ESD-1 - stop the pumps and close the manifold valves on both sides. Transfer ceases. Triggered manually from either end or automatically by tank level, pressure, gas detection or fire.
Drain and reduce inventory in the transfer line so far as the time available allows.

ESD-2 - the release stage. The coupling's isolating valves close first, then the coupling parts at its designed point. Initiation is manual, or automatic from mooring load or vessel position monitoring exceeding its limits.
After release - both sides are purged with nitrogen, the parted hose end is made safe, and personnel stay clear of the release zone while residual liquid boils off.

Before transfer the ESD link must be connected and function-tested, the coupling confirmed armed and certified, communications and agreed emergency signals established, and the release covered in the bunkering plan and drilled.

blocks.p: Four processes are named, so the examiner is marking four visible blocks. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write one long essay on LNG bunkering and leave the marker hunting for the four headings. Head each one exactly as printed. One short framing paragraph first is worth having - it lets you name the IGF Code, ISO 20519 and the ESD link once, so all four processes can then refer back to them without repetition.

blocks.h: The idea that ties the four together

blocks.p: Three of the four are about vapour and temperature, not liquid. That is the whole point. In LNG work the danger is rarely the liquid sitting in a tank - it is the gas you create by doing something too fast. Gassing up removes an atmosphere that would freeze or accumulate; cooling down prevents the flash-off that a warm tank would produce; vapour management disposes of the gas that filling inevitably generates. The emergency release is the fourth because it accepts that despite all of that, the connection may still have to be broken - and even then the design goal is the same, to part the line without releasing what is inside it. The order is also the order of the operation: you cannot cool a tank you have not gassed up, and you cannot fill one you have not cooled.

blocks.h: Why gassing up comes before cooling down

blocks.p: Because the freezing problem has to be solved while everything is still warm. Inert gas from a generator carries carbon dioxide, which becomes a solid well above LNG temperature. Introduce liquid into a tank that still holds carbon dioxide and you produce dry ice inside valves, strainers and spray lines - exactly where you least want a blockage. Gassing up removes it first. Nitrogen is a gentler problem but a persistent one: it will not freeze, but because it does not condense it stays in the vapour space, builds pressure, and thins the gas going to the engines. So gassing up is not a formality before the real work; it is what makes the cooling stage survivable.

ul: Reversing the order - cooling down before gassing up. Liquid must not enter a tank still holding inert gas.
Saying gassing up removes air. Air was removed earlier by inerting; gassing up removes the inert gas or nitrogen and replaces it with methane vapour.
Describing cooling down as "filling slowly". It is spray cooling through nozzles at a controlled rate of temperature fall, not a slow bulk fill.
Treating venting as normal vapour management. It is a last resort; the vapour return line is the primary route and methane venting carries a real environmental penalty.
Describing the emergency release coupling as a hose that simply breaks. Its defining feature is the interlocked isolating valves that close before separation.
Conflating ESD-1 and ESD-2. Stopping the transfer and parting the connection are two different stages, and ESD-2 follows ESD-1.

blocks.p:
"Why not use inert gas from the generator and go straight to loading?" Carbon dioxide in the inert gas freezes at LNG temperature and blocks the system. That single sentence is what the gassing-up limb is really testing.

"What limits how fast you can bunker?" Not the pump - the vapour handling capacity and the tank pressure limit. Bunkering is paced by where the gas can go.

"The bunker vessel starts to drift. What happens first?" ESD-1 stops the transfer and closes the manifold valves; only then does ESD-2 operate the release coupling. Going straight to "the hose disconnects" misses the sequence.

"You loaded a different LNG on top of your heel. What is the risk?" Stratification and rollover - a sudden mixing of layers of different density releasing a large volume of vapour and spiking tank pressure.

ul: What is the purpose of gassing up? To displace inert gas or nitrogen with methane vapour before liquid is admitted, chiefly to remove carbon dioxide that would freeze.
Why is warm vapour admitted at the top of the tank? It is lighter than nitrogen, so it layers above and pushes the heavier gas out through the bottom line.
What is the approximate temperature of LNG? About minus 162 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure.
What is the primary route for displaced vapour during bunkering? The vapour return line back to the bunkering facility.
What does an emergency release coupling do that an ordinary quick-release does not? Its interlocked isolating valves close before the coupling parts, containing the line inventory.
What links the two ESD systems? A ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore ESD link, so that shutdown on either side acts on both.

blocks.p: CLEAN - CHILL - CONTROL - CUT. Clean the atmosphere (step 2, gassing up). Chill the structure (step 3, cooling down). Control the pressure (step 4, vapour management). Cut the connection safely if it all goes wrong (step 5, emergency release). Step 1 is the framework they all sit in. The four Cs run in the same order as the operation itself.

Finally, the ESD-1 then ESD-2 ordering is presented as the standard arrangement, because the precise trigger logic is set by the equipment maker's design and by the agreed bunkering plan.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Framework: SOLAS II-1 part G and the IGF Code for the ship; ISO 20519 for the bunkering operation; a two-stage ESD with the delivery facility and receiving ship joined by an ESD link. GASSING UP - before any liquid: replace inert gas or nitrogen with methane vapour, because carbon dioxide in inert gas FREEZES at LNG temperature and blocks the system, and nitrogen is non-condensable and builds pressure. LNG through a vaporiser, warm vapour admitted at the TOP, heavier inert gas pushed out at the bottom to the vent mast; stop when hydrocarbon content is up and carbon dioxide is down to the ship's specified values. COOLING DOWN - spray LNG through top nozzles at a controlled rate of temperature fall to about minus 162 degrees, to avoid thermal shock and the flash-off a warm tank would produce; then bulk fill at a low initial rate. VAPOUR MANAGEMENT - vapour return line first; then consumption, reliquefaction or a gas combustion unit; venting is a LAST RESORT. Watch tank pressure against the relief setting, level trips, and rollover when loading onto a heel of different density. EMERGENCY RELEASE - ESD-1 stops pumps and closes manifold valves; ESD-2 then closes the coupling's INTERLOCKED ISOLATING VALVES BEFORE the halves part, so the line inventory is contained; purge with nitrogen and secure the parted end. The ESD link must be function-tested before transfer.
critical_numbers: LNG is carried at about minus 162 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure
Cooldown rate is limited to the maximum rate of temperature fall set by the tank designer and class - a ship-specific figure, not a universal one
Gassing-up completion is judged on hydrocarbon and carbon dioxide percentages specified in the ship's manual for that containment system
Two ESD stages: ESD-1 stops transfer, ESD-2 releases the coupling

Air went out at inerting; gassing up removes the inert gas or nitrogen, chiefly because carbon dioxide would freeze at LNG temperature. Second trap: treating venting as normal vapour management - the vapour return line is the primary route and venting is a last resort.

questions.understand_first: Three of these four processes are about vapour and temperature, not liquid, and that is the key to the whole question. In LNG work the hazard is rarely the liquid sitting in a tank - it is the gas you generate by doing something too quickly. Gassing up removes an atmosphere that would freeze solid or refuse to condense; cooling down prevents the violent boil-off a warm tank would produce; vapour management disposes of the gas that filling inevitably creates, and is what actually paces the transfer. The fourth accepts that the connection may still have to be broken, and even then the design aim is unchanged: part the line without releasing what is inside it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the LNG bunkering question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the framework - IGF Code, ISO 20519, the ESD link. 2 gassing up. 3 cooling down. 4 vapour management. 5 the emergency release coupling procedure.
retrieval_cards.why: Framing first, then the four printed processes in the printed order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a tank be gassed up before LNG is admitted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because carbon dioxide in inert gas freezes solid at LNG temperature and would block valves, strainers and spray lines; and nitrogen, while it will not freeze, is non-condensable, so it accumulates in the vapour space, raises pressure and thins the gas supplied to the engines.
retrieval_cards.why: The freezing point is what the limb is really testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is gassing up carried out, and why at the top of the tank?
retrieval_cards.answer: LNG is passed through a vaporiser to give warm methane vapour, admitted at the top of the tank. Methane vapour is lighter than nitrogen, so it layers above and pushes the heavier inert gas down and out through the bottom liquid line to the vent mast or back to the supply.
retrieval_cards.why: Density difference is what makes the displacement work.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is cooling down for, and how is it done?
retrieval_cards.answer: To bring tank, pipework and manifold gradually to about minus 162 degrees Celsius, avoiding thermal shock to the structure and the violent flash-off that LNG produces on warm surfaces. Done by spraying small controlled quantities of LNG through nozzles at the top, within the rate of temperature fall set by the designer and class.
retrieval_cards.why: Spray cooling at a controlled rate, not a slow bulk fill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Rank the routes for vapour during bunkering.
retrieval_cards.answer: Vapour return line to the bunker source first; then consumption in engines, boilers or generators; then reliquefaction where fitted; then a gas combustion unit for surplus. Controlled venting to the vent mast is a last resort only, because methane is a potent greenhouse gas.
retrieval_cards.why: Venting last is the point - it is not routine practice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes an emergency release coupling different from an ordinary quick-release?
retrieval_cards.answer: Its interlocked isolating valves close before the two halves separate, so the liquid held in the transfer line is contained and the loss of LNG or natural gas on activation is minimised.
retrieval_cards.why: The valves, not the parting, are the safety feature.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the emergency release sequence.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESD-1 stops the pumps and closes the manifold valves on both sides, ending transfer. Line inventory is drained as far as time allows. ESD-2 then closes the coupling's isolating valves and the coupling parts. Both sides purge with nitrogen and the parted end is secured.
retrieval_cards.why: Two stages, in order - stop first, part second.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What actually limits the rate at which a ship can be bunkered with LNG?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not the pump, but the vapour handling capacity and the tank pressure limit. The rate is paced by where the displaced and boil-off gas can go - principally the vapour return line - and by keeping pressure below the relief valve setting.
retrieval_cards.why: Bunkering speed is a vapour problem, not a liquid one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instruments govern LNG-fuelled ships and their bunkering?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS chapter II-1 part G with the IGF Code (resolution MSC.391(95)) for the ship's design, arrangement and operation; ISO 20519 for the bunkering operation, covering equipment, procedures, competence and the LNG bunker delivery note.
retrieval_cards.why: One for the ship, one for the transfer.

blocks.h: 1. What the Enhanced Survey Programme is

blocks.p: The ESP is a mandatory regime of intensified hull inspection for the two ship types whose structural failures have historically been catastrophic. It sits in the 2011 ESP Code, adopted as resolution A.1049(27) on 30 November 2011 and made compulsory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2. Annex A covers bulk carriers, Annex B oil tankers, each split between single- and double-skin or double- and non-double-hull construction, and the Code is closely aligned with IACS Unified Requirement Z10.

It works by requiring, in addition to the ordinary periodical survey, a planned programme of close-up survey of critical structure within arm's reach, thickness measurement by an approved firm, and tank testing - all governed by a Survey Programme agreed with the Administration or its recognized organization before the renewal survey begins.

blocks.h: 2. What a Condition Assessment Programme survey is

blocks.p: CAP is a voluntary, additional classification-society service, carried out at the owner's request. Nothing in SOLAS or MARPOL requires it. Its purpose is commercial: it produces a numerical rating of the ship's actual condition, judged not against the minimum acceptable standard but against a new-build standard, and its scope is selectable - hull, machinery, cargo systems, or a combination. Owners buy it because charterers, oil-major vetting inspectors, buyers and financiers want an independent grading of an older ship, and it involves far more extensive gauging and testing than an ESP survey does.

blocks.p: In one line: ESP is a floor and CAP is a grade. CAP does not replace, extend or satisfy any statutory or class survey, and a good rating does not maintain class.

blocks.h: 4. Documents required to plan the survey

ul: The Survey Programme itself, developed by the owner and agreed with the Administration or RO before the survey begins, with the completed survey planning questionnaire.

Main structural plans of cargo and ballast tanks - scantling drawings, including identification of high-tensile steel, without which gauging results cannot be judged against the right diminution allowance.
Details of the means of access and the safe access plan (see below).
Evidence that the thickness measurement firm is approved by the society and its operators qualified.
The agenda and record of the survey planning meeting held before work starts between the attending surveyor, the owner's representative and the thickness measurement firm.
The Survey Report File - kept on board and at the owner's office - containing reports of structural surveys, the condition evaluation report and thickness measurement reports.
Previous repair history, and the history of cargoes and ballast carried, noting corrosive cargoes and tanks used for ballast.
Information on the corrosion prevention system - coating type and condition, anodes, and the standard of maintenance - together with the Coating Technical File for ballast tanks.
For tankers, the extent of inert gas plant use and the tank cleaning procedures followed.
Inspection reports by the ship's personnel on structural deterioration, fractures, leakage in bulkheads and piping, and coating breakdown.
Reports of port State control inspections recording structural deficiencies, and relevant safety management system records and non-conformities.
Any other information helping identify suspect areas and critical structural areas.

The means of access provided for each space and each area of close-up survey - permanent staging and walkways, temporary staging, rafts or boats, portable ladders, hydraulic arm vehicles, movable platforms, or remote inspection techniques where the society accepts them.
Confirmation that each means brings the surveyor within arm's reach of the structure to be examined.

The conditions attached to rafting - adequate clearance beneath the deckhead, controlled water level, lighting, attendance, lifejackets, and the requirement that the coating be in good condition with no structural failure in the space.
Enclosed space entry arrangements - ventilation, atmosphere testing for oxygen, hydrocarbons and toxic gases, gas-freeing, permit to work, standby personnel, and rescue equipment.
Lighting of an approved and adequate standard, and communication arrangements between the survey party and the responsible officer.
Cleaning and preparation - tanks cleaned, de-scaled and sufficiently free of water, sludge and residue for the structure to be seen.
Safety equipment and personal protective equipment, and the identity of the responsible person attending to supervise.
It is the owner who must provide the facilities for safe execution, and the surveyor may decline to proceed if they are not in place.

blocks.p: Three printed limbs, and the marks are unevenly available. Limb (a) is where the real discrimination happens, because the difference is conceptual, not a matter of listing two definitions. Limbs (b) and (c) are pure recall and reward organised lists - so give them structure rather than a stream of items. Splitting (b) into documents needed to plan and records of the ship's history and condition makes it far easier to write completely under pressure, and it is how the survey programme itself is organised.

ESP asks a pass/fail question; CAP asks a scoring question. The ESP exists to establish that the structure is still at or above the minimum standard the ship must meet to hold its certificates - a floor. CAP exists to say how far above that floor the ship actually sits, measured against a new-build standard - a grade. That single distinction generates every other difference: because ESP answers a legal question it is mandatory, flag-driven and hull-focused, and failure stops the ship trading. Because CAP answers a commercial question it is voluntary, owner-requested, scope-selectable, and failure costs charters rather than certificates.

blocks.h: The abbreviation trap that decides this question

blocks.p: CAP is not CAS. The Condition Assessment Programme is the voluntary classification-society grading described above. The Condition Assessment Scheme is a mandatory regime under MARPOL Annex I applying to single-hull oil tankers, adopted by IMO resolution. A candidate who answers limb (a) by describing CAS has answered the wrong question and has, worse, said that the thing is mandatory when the question is precisely about a voluntary scheme. If you are asked to distinguish ESP from CAP and you find yourself writing "MARPOL", stop - you have taken the wrong turning.

blocks.h: Why the paperwork in limb (b) exists

blocks.p: None of it is bureaucracy for its own sake, and saying why earns more than the list alone. A thickness reading is meaningless without the scantling drawing that says what the plate started at and whether it is high-tensile steel, because HTS carries a different diminution allowance. The cargo and ballast history tells the surveyor where to look, since a tank that has carried corrosive cargo or has been used for ballast corrodes differently. The coating condition and the Coating Technical File predict where wastage will appear next. And the Survey Report File makes the ship's structural condition a trend rather than a snapshot - which is the whole point of an enhanced programme.

ul: Describing CAP as a statutory requirement, or confusing it with the Condition Assessment Scheme under MARPOL Annex I.
Saying CAP replaces or extends class or statutory surveys. It does neither, and a good rating does not maintain class.
Saying the ESP applies to all ships. It applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers.
Omitting that the Survey Programme must be agreed before the survey starts, and that a planning meeting is held.
Treating the safe access plan as a generic risk assessment. It is specific - which means of access, for which space, reaching which structure.
Forgetting that thickness measurement must be carried out by a firm approved by the society, not by the crew.

blocks.p:
"The owner has a CAP 1 rating. Can the special survey be relaxed?" No. CAP has no statutory effect whatever; the ESP survey stands in full.

"Which is more demanding?" In gauging volume and testing, CAP usually is - but it is the voluntary one. Demanding and mandatory are different axes, and that is the point of the comparison.

"When may a tank be rafted for close-up survey?" Only under conditions - clearance beneath the deckhead, controlled water level, adequate lighting and attendance, and the coating in good condition with no structural failure. "Whenever the tank is flooded" is wrong.

"Why does the surveyor want to know about high-tensile steel?" Because the permissible diminution differs, so the same measured thickness can be acceptable in one plate and a rejection in another.

ul: Which resolution is the ESP Code, and what makes it mandatory? Resolution A.1049(27), the 2011 ESP Code, made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2.
Which ships does it apply to? Bulk carriers and oil tankers - Annex A and Annex B of the Code respectively.
What is a close-up survey? Examination of structural detail within arm's reach of the surveyor.
Who may carry out thickness measurement? A firm approved by the classification society, with qualified operators.
What is in the Survey Report File? Reports of structural surveys, the condition evaluation report and the thickness measurement reports.
Is CAP required by any convention? No. It is a voluntary classification-society service requested by the owner.
Who is responsible for safe access during survey? The owner, who must provide the facilities; the surveyor may decline to proceed without them.

blocks.p: FLOOR versus GRADE, then PLAN - HISTORY - ACCESS. Limb (a) is floor against grade (steps 1 to 3). Limb (b) splits into what you need to plan the survey - programme, drawings, approved gauging firm, planning meeting (step 4) - and what tells you the ship's history and present condition - report file, repairs, cargo and ballast, coatings, crew and port State reports (step 5). Limb (c) is access: how do you physically get within arm's reach, and get out again safely (step 6).

blocks.p: The identity of the ESP Code is primary-verified from the IMO resolution record: resolution A.1049(27), adopted 30 November 2011, mandatory under SOLAS regulation XI-1/2, with Annex A for bulk carriers and Annex B for oil tankers and the amendment chain running to MSC.461(101) in force 1 January 2021. What is weaker, and is stated at that level, is the detail. MIW holds no licensed copy of the ESP Code or of SOLAS, so the documentation list in limb (b) and the safe access content in limb (c) are assembled from classification-society restatements of the Code's survey programme requirements rather than read in the Code's own annexes; they are consistent across societies but they are not quoted from the instrument. Two figures are deliberately withheld. Gross tonnage thresholds for application are stated differently by different secondary sources, so the answer names the ship types and asserts no tonnage. questions.understand_first: The two regimes answer different questions, and everything else follows from that. The Enhanced Survey Programme asks whether the structure is still at or above the minimum standard the ship must meet to keep its certificates - a floor, checked because the law requires it. A Condition Assessment Programme survey asks how far above that floor the ship actually sits, measured against a new-build standard - a grade, bought because a charterer or a buyer wants an independent opinion on an ageing ship. So the more demanding survey of the two is usually the voluntary one, which feels backwards until you see that demanding and mandatory are separate axes.
