blocks.h: 1. Secure the evidence and establish the facts

ul: Do not dress, grind or blend the crack. Material removed before assessment destroys the evidence class, the underwriter and the root-cause investigation all need.
Record it. Photographs and video with a scale in frame, and a dimensioned sketch.

Locate it precisely - blade number from the stamping on the boss, pressure or suction face, radial position as a fraction of the blade radius, distance from the leading or trailing edge and from tip and root, and the crack's length and orientation.
Examine the whole propeller, not just the one blade - the remaining blades, the leading and trailing edges, the tips, the boss, the keyway and the fairing cone. A crack is rarely isolated.
Look for related damage - rudder, stern frame, rope guard, stern tube seal, hull marks - which would point to contact or grounding.

Assemble the service history - vibration or unusual noise, shaft power and revolution anomalies, any grounding, ice contact or rope entanglement, stern tube oil analysis and the planned maintenance record.

Clean the area only as far as the surveyor permits, then carry out liquid dye penetrant testing. Propellers are cast in non-ferromagnetic alloys - nickel-aluminium bronze or manganese bronze - so magnetic particle inspection cannot be used. Where depth must be established, eddy current or ultrasonic techniques are applied.
Have the testing done by a qualified operator from an approved firm and obtain a written report.
Establish what the defect actually is: a genuine fatigue crack, a casting defect, or cavitation erosion pitting that resembles cracking. The three have different consequences and different causes.

Inform the Master first, then report to the Company - the technical superintendent and, under the ISM Code, the Designated Person Ashore - and raise it in the safety management system as a hazardous occurrence or non-conformity so that it enters the analysis and corrective-action process.

The report must be factual and complete: description and precise location, dimensions, NDT method and result, photographs and sketch, propeller particulars (maker, material, drawing and serial number, diameter and pitch), relevant service history, and the effect on the dry-dock programme and undocking date.

State the options and a recommendation, with the implications of each for cost and time - but recognise the division of responsibility: the Chief Engineer establishes the facts and recommends; the Company decides and instructs.
Request instructions, and confirm who will liaise with class, the repairer and the underwriter.

blocks.h: 4. Involve classification and settle the repair

ul: Notify the classification society and request the attending surveyor to examine. The owner is under a duty to report any damage or defect which affects or may affect classification, and concealing it puts class - and with it the statutory certificates and the insurance - at risk.

The surveyor assesses the crack against the society's rules. Acceptance depends heavily on where on the blade it lies: the highly stressed region is the most restricted and repairs there are limited or prohibited, while damage near the tip is treated far more permissively. ISO 484 governs the tolerances against which repaired geometry is judged.

The possible outcomes are: accept as found; grind out and blend to a smooth radius within permitted limits; weld repair by an approved procedure; crop and re-form; or replace the blade or the propeller.

Where a repair is done it must be by a class-approved repairer to an approved welding procedure with the pre-heat and post-weld heat treatment the alloy requires, followed by re-testing, a check of pitch and geometry, and static balancing.
Obtain the surveyor's endorsement. If the repair is deferred, expect a condition of class with a time limit rather than a clean survey.

Consider separately whether the occurrence is reportable to the flag Administration. That turns on its cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected - damage arising from a grounding or contact is reportable; wastage found at a routine docking generally is not.

blocks.h: 5. Insurance and preservation of the claim

ul: Through the Company, notify the hull and machinery underwriters, and the P&I club if any third-party element arises, and arrange attendance of the underwriter's surveyor before repairs begin.

Whether a claim lies depends on the cause. Damage from an insured peril such as contact or grounding is recoverable; ordinary wear and tear and cavitation erosion are not, and a latent defect is recoverable only so far as the policy provides for it.
Do not commit to a repair method or cost without the underwriter's agreement where a claim is contemplated, and retain removed material and samples for metallurgical examination.

Establish the cause: cavitation erosion; fatigue initiating at cavitation pitting or a casting defect acting as a stress raiser; impact with a submerged object or ice; dezincification of manganese bronze; galvanic attack where anodes or the impressed current system are defective; or sustained overload from heavy running or excessive astern working.
Act on it - review hull and propeller roughness, fouling and polishing intervals, confirm cathodic protection is functioning, monitor shaft vibration, and review astern working and heavy running.

Close the loop: file the NDT and survey reports, repair procedure, welder qualifications and balancing record; update the machinery history, planned maintenance system and underwater inspection schedule; feed the lessons through the safety management system; and hand over fully.

blocks.p: The command is state the steps, so the answer must be a sequence, not an essay about propellers. Six headed steps in a defensible order will outscore a longer piece of prose every time. Notice what the question actually asks: it is a management question with a technical trigger. The examiner wants to see that a Chief Engineer knows who must be told, in what order, and what must not be touched in the meantime. Metallurgy earns marks only where it changes a decision.

blocks.h: The instinct you have to suppress

blocks.p: The engineer's reflex on finding a surface crack in a dock, with the undocking date approaching, is to dress it out and carry on. That reflex is the most expensive mistake available here. Grinding the crack away before anyone has seen it destroys three things at once: the class surveyor's ability to assess what was actually there, the underwriter's ability to accept a claim, and the root-cause investigation that would stop it happening on the sister ship. The propeller can be repaired later; none of that evidence can be recovered. So the first step is not a repair step at all - it is to stop, record, and report.

blocks.h: Why location on the blade decides almost everything

blocks.p: A propeller blade is not uniformly stressed. Bending stress from thrust and torque is greatest towards the root, and the blade is thinnest towards the tip and the edges, so a crack of the same length means very different things depending on where it is. Classification rules divide the blade into zones accordingly: in the highly stressed region, welding is restricted or not permitted at all and the realistic outcomes are limited grinding or blade replacement; near the tip the same defect may be blended out without difficulty. This is why the answer must record blade number, face, radius and distance from the edge before anything else - those four facts, not the crack's length, are what determine the outcome.

ul: Proposing magnetic particle inspection. Propellers are nickel-aluminium or manganese bronze and are not ferromagnetic, so MPI simply does not work. Use dye penetrant.
Grinding or welding before class attends and before the extent is established.
Reporting to the Company but not to class, or assuming the superintendent will do it.
Treating every crack as a claim. Cavitation erosion and ordinary wear are not insured perils.
Deciding the repair yourself. The Chief Engineer recommends; the Company instructs and class approves.
Omitting balancing and geometry check after repair - a repaired blade that is out of pitch or out of balance introduces vibration and a new fatigue problem.
Stopping at the repair and never establishing the cause, which guarantees a repeat.

blocks.p:
"Why not MPI?" Because the material is not ferromagnetic. If you cannot answer this you have shown you have never actually stood at a propeller in a dock.

"The dock is due to flood tomorrow. What do you do?" Report and get class to attend. Commercial pressure does not change the sequence, and undocking with an unreported defect affecting class is a far worse outcome than a delay.

"Is this a general average or a hull claim?" Neither is automatic - it depends entirely on cause. Establish that first.

"You blended out the crack and it looked fine. Any problem?" Yes - the blade geometry and pitch may now be outside tolerance, the blade is out of balance with the others, and you have removed the evidence. Blending is permitted only within limits and with class agreement.

"Must you report it to the flag State?" It depends on cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected - not automatically.

ul: Which NDT method for a bronze propeller, and why? Dye penetrant - the alloy is not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle inspection is unusable.
What four facts locate the defect? Blade number, pressure or suction face, radial position, and distance from the leading or trailing edge.
Who approves a propeller weld repair? The classification society, and it must be carried out by an approved repairer to an approved procedure.
What is done after a blade repair? Re-testing, a pitch and geometry check against tolerance, and static balancing.
What happens if the repair is deferred? A condition of class with a time limit may be imposed.
Name three causes of blade cracking. Cavitation erosion leading to fatigue, impact with a submerged object, and a casting defect acting as a stress raiser.
Who do you tell first on board? The Master, then the Company and the Designated Person Ashore.

blocks.p: STOP - TEST - TELL - CLASS - CLAIM - CAUSE. Stop and preserve the evidence (step 1). Test to establish what it really is (2). Tell the Master and the Company (3). Class attends and settles the repair (4). Claim - notify underwriters before repairing (5). Cause - find it, fix it, record it (6). The order matters and is itself examinable: everything that could destroy evidence comes after the people who need that evidence have been told.

questions.understand_first: The instinct on finding a crack in a dock, with the undocking date approaching, is to dress it out and carry on. That instinct is the whole trap. Grinding the defect away before it has been seen destroys three separate things at once - the class surveyor's assessment, the insurer's ability to accept a claim, and the root-cause work that would stop it recurring on the sister ship. The propeller can be repaired later; none of that evidence can be recovered. So this is not really a repair question. It is a question about the order in which people are told, and about the fact that a Chief Engineer establishes facts and recommends while the Company decides and class approves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the propeller crack question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 secure the evidence and establish the facts. 2 establish the nature and extent by NDT. 3 report to the Company. 4 involve classification and settle the repair. 5 insurance and preservation of the claim. 6 root cause, prevention and close-out.
retrieval_cards.why: Everything that could destroy evidence comes after the people who need it have been told.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can magnetic particle inspection not be used on a propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because marine propellers are cast in non-ferromagnetic alloys - nickel-aluminium bronze or manganese bronze - and magnetic particle inspection requires a ferromagnetic material. Liquid dye penetrant is the standard surface method, with eddy current or ultrasonic where depth must be established.
retrieval_cards.why: A single fact that shows whether the candidate has really been at a propeller.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must the crack not be ground out before class attends?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it simultaneously destroys the surveyor's ability to assess what was there, the underwriter's ability to accept a claim, and the root-cause investigation. The propeller can be repaired later; the evidence cannot be recovered.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial pressure to do exactly this is the point of the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which four facts locate the defect?
retrieval_cards.answer: Blade number from the boss stamping; whether it is on the pressure or the suction face; the radial position as a fraction of blade radius; and the distance from the leading or trailing edge. These, not the crack's length, determine the repair outcome.
retrieval_cards.why: Position on the blade governs what class will permit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the owner's duty to the classification society here?
retrieval_cards.answer: To report any damage or defect which affects or may affect classification, and to have the surveyor attend. A repair requires an approved repairer working to an approved procedure, followed by re-examination, a geometry and pitch check, and balancing.
retrieval_cards.why: Concealment puts class, the statutory certificates and the insurance at risk.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who decides what happens to the propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not the Chief Engineer. The CE establishes the facts, reports and recommends; the Company decides and instructs; the classification society approves the repair and endorses it. Confusing those roles is a management failure, not a technical one.
retrieval_cards.why: The question is about handling the situation, not fixing the blade.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must be done after a blade repair is completed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Re-testing by NDT, a check of pitch and blade geometry against tolerance, and static balancing - then the surveyor's endorsement. A repaired blade out of pitch or out of balance introduces vibration and a fresh fatigue problem.
retrieval_cards.why: The repair is not finished when the welding stops.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the likely causes of propeller blade cracking.
retrieval_cards.answer: Cavitation erosion, and fatigue initiating at cavitation pitting or at a casting defect acting as a stress raiser; impact with a submerged object or ice; dezincification of manganese bronze; galvanic attack where anodes or the impressed current system are defective; and sustained overload from heavy running or excessive astern working.
retrieval_cards.why: Cause drives both the insurance position and the prevention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is this automatically an insurance claim and a reportable casualty?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither is automatic. Recoverability depends on cause and on the policy - an insured peril such as contact or grounding may be recoverable, while ordinary wear and cavitation erosion are not. Reportability to the Administration depends on the cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected.
retrieval_cards.why: The question gives no cause, so both must be stated as conditional.

blocks.h: 1. a) What FSA is, and who it is for

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is set out in MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) for use in the IMO rule-making process, of 9 April 2018. The title states its purpose: a structured, auditable methodology by which the Organization decides whether, and how, to regulate a hazard, balancing safety benefit against cost. It is not a shipboard risk assessment or a permit-to-work system. The question is therefore how a proportionate rule for this cargo was, and is being, arrived at.

blocks.h: 2. Step 1 - identifying the hazards of this cargo

ul: Thermal runaway - an exothermic internal reaction that becomes self-sustaining and generates its own oxidant, so it cannot be smothered and continues without external air;
propagation cell to cell and module to module, and thence vehicle to vehicle in a close stow;
initiators - internal cell defects, mechanical damage in handling or lashing, over-charge, high state of charge on shipment, charging on board;
vent gas - flammable and toxic, able to accumulate in an enclosed vehicle space and produce a gas explosion rather than a simple fire;
re-ignition hours or days after apparent extinction, defeating a normal fire-out judgement;

mis-declaration and concealment - cells as cargo may be undeclared or wrongly classified, and a battery electric vehicle is not a labelled package at all, so the energy is invisible to the stowage plan.

blocks.h: 3. Step 2 - assessing the risk on a ro-ro deck

blocks.p: Risk is frequency times consequence, estimated from casualty returns, incident and near-miss data, cell testing and fire modelling - with the Rev.2 requirement that the reliability, uncertainty and validity of that data be assessed and reported rather than assumed.

ul: Frequency is low per vehicle but rising with fleet electrification, and exposure is concentrated - one deck may hold thousands of units;

consequence escalates because a ro-ro space is a large undivided volume, vehicles stowed centimetres apart, with no cargo-hold fire divisions and ramps and ventilation trunks carrying heat and smoke between decks;
on a ro-pax the dominant risk is to life; on a pure car and truck carrier it is total loss of the ship, and a series of well-known casualties supplied the evidence;
manual firefighting on a loaded deck is near impossible, so the model must assume fixed systems and boundaries are what will actually be available.

blocks.h: 4. Steps 3 and 4 - risk control options and whether they pay

blocks.p: Risk control options are generated and grouped, then tested by cost-benefit assessment using indices such as the cost of averting a fatality, so a measure is recommended only where the safety gain justifies the cost across the world fleet:

ul: detection - earlier, better-located, individually identifiable so the seat of fire is known, with combined smoke and heat sensing;
suppression - drencher and water-based systems of adequate coverage and capacity, aligned with detection sections so the right section operates;
containment - insulated boundaries, ventilation shut-down and control of openings;
operational and design - state-of-charge limits on shipment, segregation and dedicated stowage, restrictions on charging at sea, video monitoring, crew procedures;
options are ranked, and those effective but disproportionately costly are rejected transparently - which is why the outcome is a specific set of measures rather than everything technically possible.

blocks.h: 5. Step 5 - what the recommendations actually became

blocks.p: The risk-based work on ro-ro fire safety - notably the EMSA FIRESAFE I and FIRESAFE II studies of fire dynamics, system performance and operational factors - entered the regulatory system in two stages:

ul: MSC.1/Circ.1615, Interim Guidelines for Minimizing the Incidence and Consequences of Fires in Ro-Ro Spaces and Special Category Spaces, carried key outcomes into guidance while mandatory work continued;

resolution MSC.550(108) then amended SOLAS chapter II-2 regulations 7 and 20 and MSC.555(108) amended FSS Code chapters 7 and 9, both adopted at MSC 108 in May 2024 and in force on 1 January 2026 - earlier in the year in which this paper was sat;

requirements include individually identifiable fixed detection with combined smoke and heat detectors, detection aligned with deluge sections, detection on weather decks used for vehicles, an effective video monitoring system with at least seven days of replay at a continuously manned control station, and A-60 boundaries on passenger ships carrying more than 36 passengers;
they apply to ships constructed on or after 1 January 2026, existing ships in scope complying not later than the first survey on or after 1 January 2028;
further amendments aimed at new energy vehicles were still in development, so the regulatory answer is partly delivered and continuing.
IMO - complete the new-energy-vehicle amendments, keep IMDG provisions current, maintain interim guidance meanwhile;
flag State and class - approve and survey the amended detection, suppression and boundary arrangements, and issue guidance ahead of the compliance dates;
shipper, manufacturer and packer - correct IMDG classification, packing and marking, state-of-charge control, testing and quality control, and no offering of damaged, defective or recalled batteries;
port and terminal - screen and refuse visibly damaged vehicles, check declared state of charge, separate electric vehicles in marshalling areas, inform the ship promptly;
ship operator - a written stowage and segregation policy, limits on charging on board, training in lithium fire behaviour, vehicle-deck drills, thermal imaging, and a plan that assumes re-ignition;

ship's staff - verify cargo against the declaration, maintain detection and drencher readiness, patrol during and after loading, and fight fire by early activation of fixed systems and boundary cooling rather than entering a loaded deck;
insurers and industry bodies - loss-prevention guidance, incident and near-miss data sharing, and premium signals rewarding compliant stowage - the same data that feeds the next FSA.

blocks.p: The 10-mark limb is a method question, and method questions are marked on whether the method is visible. Naming the five steps and then walking the cargo through them is what separates a top answer from a general essay about battery fires. Step 5 is where most candidates stop short: an FSA that produces no recommendation has not been applied, so ending with the actual resolutions is what closes the loop.

Before FSA, IMO regulation was largely reactive - a casualty happened, and a rule followed. FSA was introduced after the Herald of Free Enterprise and Piper Alpha era to allow the Organization to act proactively and proportionately, on evidence rather than on the emotional weight of the most recent disaster, and to be able to say publicly why a proposed rule was or was not worth its cost. That is why the Guidelines insist on auditability, traceability and the explicit reporting of uncertainty: an FSA is as much an accountability document as a technical one.

blocks.h: The lithium hazard in engineering terms

blocks.p: Thermal runaway begins when a cell's internal temperature passes the point at which exothermic decomposition of the electrolyte and cathode outpaces heat loss. The decomposition liberates oxygen from the cathode material, which is why the reaction sustains itself without air and why smothering agents - CO2, foam blanket, an inert atmosphere - do not stop it. Cooling is the only lever the ship holds, and it works by removing heat from cells that have not yet reached onset temperature, so its real objective is to stop propagation to neighbouring vehicles rather than to extinguish the cell already in runaway. That is also why re-ignition is normal rather than surprising: the cells that were merely heated may still cross the threshold hours later.

blocks.h: Vehicles, containers and packages are three different regulatory problems

ul: Cells and batteries as cargo - dangerous goods under the IMDG Code, class 9, with UN numbers such as 3480 and 3481 for lithium-ion and 3090 and 3091 for lithium-metal, subject to packing, marking, documentation and segregation.
Batteries in or with equipment - the same UN family but different provisions, and often carried under exceptions.

A battery electric vehicle - carried as a vehicle, not as a declared dangerous goods package. This is the regulatory gap: the ship may know exactly how many tonnes of declared lithium cells she has in containers, and not know how much energy is sitting on the vehicle deck.
Describing FSA as a shipboard risk assessment. Read the circular's title.
Listing the five steps and then never using them - a hazard essay wearing an FSA hat.
Saying water must never be used on a lithium fire. Cooling and boundary protection with copious water is the accepted tactic.
Saying the fire can be smothered with CO2. The reaction supplies its own oxidant.
Declaring the fire out when flames stop. Re-ignition must be assumed and monitored for.
Treating a battery electric vehicle as though it were declared dangerous goods, or vice versa.
'In vehicles and containers and in RORO ships' - three carriage modes are named deliberately, and an answer that only discusses containers has ignored a third of the question.
'Application of formal safety assessment' - the mark is in the application, not the definition.
Limb (b) says stakeholders, plural. An answer confined to what the ship's staff should do cannot score well; the chain begins at the cell manufacturer.
A car on your vehicle deck is smoking. What are your first four actions?
Why will CO2 not put out a lithium-ion fire?
How would you know a battery electric vehicle had been loaded?
What does 'individually identifiable' mean in a detection system, and why does it matter here?
When can you say this fire is out?

blocks.p: The method as a funnel: what could go wrong, how bad and how often, what could we do, is it worth it, what do we recommend. The hazard in four words that each defeat a normal tactic: self-oxidising, propagating, venting, re-igniting. The remedy chain for limb (b) runs down the supply chain: regulator, class, shipper, terminal, operator, ship.

blocks.p: Two limitations are stated rather than concealed. First, no dedicated published IMO Formal Safety Assessment study on lithium batteries in ro-ro carriage was located. The answer therefore explains how the FSA method applies to this cargo and identifies the FIRESAFE programme and the resulting amendments as the risk-based work that was actually done; it does not assert that a formal FSA submission on lithium batteries exists. Second, MIW holds no licensed SOLAS or FSS Code, so the amendment content rests on an authoritative class-society restatement. The dates matter unusually here: MSC.550(108) and MSC.555(108) had been in force only since the start of that year at the date of this sitting, and the further new energy vehicle amendments were still in development - so an answer written today must not project the later position back onto March 2026.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is thermal runaway in a lithium-ion cell so difficult to fight on a vehicle deck?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is self-sustaining and does not require external oxygen, so smothering does not stop it; it propagates cell to cell; it vents flammable and toxic gas that can accumulate and explode; and it can re-ignite hours or days after apparent extinction.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention and when it bit

blocks.p: The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 was adopted at a diplomatic conference in Hong Kong, China in May 2009 and entered into force on 26 June 2025 - more than fifteen years later. The delay is explained by Article 17, which imposes a triple condition: twenty-four months after not less than 15 States have consented to be bound, whose combined fleets are not less than 40 per cent of world gross tonnage, and whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage - the third condition making the Convention impossible to bring into force without the major recycling States. At entry into force there were 24 Parties representing about 57 per cent of world tonnage, including Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Turkiye.

ul: An Inventory of Hazardous Materials in three parts - materials in the structure and equipment, operationally generated wastes, and stores - with Parts II and III completed before recycling.
Survey and certification: an International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and, after a final survey, an International Ready for Recycling Certificate.

Application to ships of 500 GT and above, except those operating throughout their life only in waters under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of the flag State (Article 3.3); existing ships must comply by 26 June 2030 or before going for recycling, whichever is earlier.
Control or prohibition of listed hazardous materials - asbestos, PCBs, ozone-depleting substances, and anti-fouling systems containing organotin compounds or cybutryne.
Recycling only at a facility authorised under the Convention in a Party State, working to a ship-specific Ship Recycling Plan, with notification of intent to recycle and a statement of completion.

blocks.h: 3. What it requires of recycling facilities

blocks.p: An IMO instrument normally regulates ships; this one reaches ashore and regulates the yard.

ul: Authorisation by the competent authority of the State, evidenced by a Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling.
A Ship Recycling Facility Plan covering worker safety and training, emergency preparedness and response, and the management of hazardous materials.
Safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot-work conditions to be established and maintained.
Controlled downstream management of the wastes removed - which is where the real burden falls.

India is one of the world's principal ship-recycling States, centred on the Alang-Sosiya yards in Gujarat, and it acceded on 28 November 2019, the Director General of Shipping depositing the instrument at the thirty-first IMO Assembly. That accession was decisive: it took the count to the required fifteen States and contributed heavily to the recycling-volume condition.

Domestically the Convention is given effect by the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019, which anticipated entry into force by six years and apply Convention standards to ships recycled in India.
The maritime administration is the competent authority, authorising yards and approving ship recycling plans.

The Recycling of Ships Act 2019 stands unaffected by the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. That Act's repeal provision, s.324(1), repeals the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838 only. The 2025 Act touches recycling only at s.17, providing for temporary registration of a vessel sought to be recycled.

Legitimacy and access to better tonnage. Owners who avoided South Asian yards on reputational grounds can now send ships to an authorised Indian facility with a defensible answer, which should raise both volume and quality of tonnage.
A level playing field. Competing recycling States must now meet the same standard, so the money India's yards spent upgrading ahead of entry into force is rewarded rather than punished on price.

Worker safety and environmental gain. Enforceable safe-for-hot-work and safe-for-entry requirements, training, protective equipment and controlled waste handling address the fatality and contamination record that has defined the industry's reputation.
Downstream industry and investment. Formalisation supports the steel re-rolling and second-hand equipment trades, and certification makes yards financeable and contractable on longer terms.

blocks.h: 6. How it stands to be impacted, and the balance

ul: Cost of compliance. Impermeable floors, containment, lifting equipment, and hazardous waste storage and treatment are capital-intensive. Small operators may not afford them, so the industry consolidates and some yards close.

Downstream waste capacity is the binding constraint. The Convention's obligations do not end at the yard gate, and treatment and disposal capacity for asbestos and other hazardous waste must exist for compliance to be real rather than documentary.

Price and leakage. Higher costs mean a lower price per light displacement tonne, creating an incentive to recycle elsewhere - including through a change of flag before the last voyage to a State outside the Convention.

Convention compliance is not European acceptance. The Convention does not expressly prohibit beaching, whereas the EU Ship Recycling Regulation maintains its own list of approved facilities on stricter terms. An Indian yard may be fully Convention-compliant and still not be EU-listed.

Enforcement is the credibility test. Authorisation has to be inspected and enforced; the industry remains under close external scrutiny, and a documentary-only regime would forfeit the reputational gain that is the main prize.

On balance, entry into force is net positive for India: it converts an early and expensive investment into a competitive advantage and legitimises the industry. The gain is conditional on downstream waste infrastructure and real enforcement keeping pace with certification - without them, the cost is incurred and the reputational benefit is not.

blocks.p: Three tasks are set inside one running stem, and candidates routinely answer only the first. Budget the paper deliberately: roughly a third on the Convention, and two thirds on India, split between benefit and impact. The word "or" in "benefit or be impacted" is not offering you a choice - it is asking for both sides and a judgement. An answer that only lists advantages has not done what was asked. Finish with an explicit balance; the archetype here is evaluation, and evaluation questions are marked on whether a reasoned conclusion actually appears.

blocks.h: The feature that makes this Convention different

blocks.p: Almost every IMO instrument regulates the ship - its construction, equipment, certificates and crew. The Hong Kong Convention is one of the very few that reaches ashore and regulates a facility on land, requiring the yard itself to be authorised, planned and inspected. That is why it took so long to bring into force: it needed the consent of States whose domestic industry, not merely whose fleet, would be regulated. And it is why Article 17's third condition exists - a recycling-volume threshold that made it impossible to bring the Convention into force over the objections of the recycling States. Read that way, India's accession in 2019 is not a footnote; it is one of the two or three events that made the Convention real.

blocks.h: The distinction that separates a good answer from a very good one

blocks.p: The Convention does not ban beaching. It requires safe and environmentally sound recycling, authorisation, planning and control - but it does not prescribe the method by which a ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation takes a stricter line and maintains its own list of approved facilities, which is why the acceptability of the Alang yards to European owners has been contested for years and is not settled by entry into force. So the accurate proposition is: Convention compliance is necessary for legitimacy but is not sufficient for European acceptance. A candidate who writes that the Convention has ended beaching, or that compliance automatically opens the EU market, has overstated it in exactly the way the examiner is watching for.

ul: Saying the Convention bans beaching, or that it makes Indian yards automatically acceptable to EU owners.
Giving the adoption year as the operative date. Adopted 2009, in force 26 June 2025 - the gap is the interesting part.
Reciting only the ship-side obligations and omitting the facility obligations, which are half the Convention.
Confusing the ICIHM (held through service life) with the Ready for Recycling Certificate (issued after the final survey, immediately before recycling).
Answering only the benefits when the question says benefit or be impacted, and giving no concluding judgement.
Attributing India's recycling law to the Merchant Shipping Act. It is the separate Recycling of Ships Act, 2019.
Quoting a percentage share of world recycling. The figures vary widely between sources; name Alang-Sosiya instead.

blocks.p:
"Did the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 change India's ship recycling law?" No. Its repeal provision, s.324(1), repeals the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838 only. The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 stands, and the 2025 Act touches recycling only at s.17, on temporary registration of a vessel sought to be recycled. This is worth knowing precisely, because a paper sat around the 2025 Act's commencement invites the assumption that everything Indian and maritime was swept up in it.

"Why did it take sixteen years?" Article 17's three conditions, and specifically the recycling-volume threshold, which required the recycling States themselves to join.

"Your ship is going for recycling next month. Which certificate?" The International Ready for Recycling Certificate, issued after the final survey, with Parts II and III of the inventory completed.

"By when must an existing ship have an inventory?" 26 June 2030, or before going for recycling, whichever comes first.

ul: When was the Convention adopted and when did it enter into force? Adopted May 2009; in force 26 June 2025.
What are the three entry-into-force conditions? Fifteen States, forty per cent of world gross tonnage, and three per cent combined annual recycling volume - then twenty-four months.
When did India accede? 28 November 2019, deposited by the Director General of Shipping at the thirty-first IMO Assembly.
Which Indian statute implements it? The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019, with the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019.
What are the three parts of the Inventory of Hazardous Materials? Materials in the structure and equipment; operationally generated wastes; and stores.
What must a recycling yard hold? A Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling, and a Ship Recycling Facility Plan.
Does the Convention prohibit beaching? No. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation applies a stricter standard through its own list of approved facilities.

blocks.p: SHIP - SHORE - INDIA - SCALES. Ship: inventory, certificates, 500 gross tonnage, 2030 (steps 1 to 2). Shore: authorisation, facility plan, safe for entry and hot work, downstream waste (step 3). India: acceded 2019, Recycling of Ships Act 2019, competent authority, untouched by the 2025 Act (step 4). Scales: weigh benefit against impact and land a judgement (steps 5 to 6). For the dates alone: adopted 2009, India acceded 2019, in force 2025, existing ships by 2030 - a decade apart each time, which makes the sequence easy to hold.

blocks.p: The Convention dates and the accession are primary-verified on the IMO's own briefings: adoption in May 2009, entry into force on 26 June 2025 with 24 Parties at about 57 per cent of world tonnage, and India's deposit on 28 November 2019. The statutory point about the 2025 Act is also strong, because s.324(1) was read in the Gazette for QP2607 Q7 and its repeal list is closed - this is the one place where a March 2026 paper could have been caught by the commencement of the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 on 15 March 2026, and it is not, because the Recycling of Ships Act 2019 is separate legislation that the repeal does not touch. What is weaker is stated as such. MIW holds no licensed copy of the Convention text, so article and appendix detail rests on IMO briefing material and classification-society guidance. No percentage share of world recycling is asserted, because published figures for India's share differ widely and none could be verified; Alang-Sosiya is named instead. The number of authorised Indian yards and of EU-listed facilities changes continuously and is deliberately not reproduced. And the commercial argument in step 6 - that compliance cost depresses the price per light displacement tonne and creates leakage to non-Party States - is presented as a mechanism, not as a measured outcome, because no price data was obtained.

FACILITIES - and this is the unusual part, an IMO convention reaching ashore: a Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling, a Ship Recycling Facility Plan, safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot-work conditions, and downstream waste management. INDIA acceded 28 NOVEMBER 2019, which took the count to fifteen; implemented by the Recycling of Ships Act 2019 and Rules 2019 - separate legislation NOT repealed by the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, whose s.324(1) repeals only the 1958 Act and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838. BENEFIT: legitimacy, better tonnage, a level playing field, worker safety, investment. IMPACT: capital cost and consolidation, downstream waste capacity as the binding constraint, price depression and leakage to non-Party flags, and the fact that the Convention DOES NOT BAN BEACHING so compliance is not EU acceptance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Hong Kong Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the Convention and when it bit. 2 what it requires of ships. 3 what it requires of recycling facilities. 4 India's position and implementing law. 5 how India benefits. 6 how it is impacted, and the balance.
retrieval_cards.why: A third on the Convention, two thirds on India - and a stated judgement at the end.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the Hong Kong Convention's key dates.
retrieval_cards.answer: Adopted at Hong Kong, China in May 2009. Entered into force 26 June 2025. India acceded 28 November 2019. Existing ships must hold an inventory by 26 June 2030, or before going for recycling, whichever is earlier.
retrieval_cards.why: Four dates roughly a decade apart - easy to hold as a sequence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the Article 17 entry-into-force conditions?
retrieval_cards.answer: Twenty-four months after not less than 15 States have consented to be bound, whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 40 per cent of world gross tonnage, and whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage.
retrieval_cards.why: The third condition is what made the recycling States indispensable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the Hong Kong Convention prohibit beaching, and does compliance open the EU market?
retrieval_cards.answer: No to both. The Convention requires safe and environmentally sound recycling, authorisation and planning, but does not prescribe how a ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation applies a stricter standard through its own list of approved facilities, so a fully compliant Indian yard may still not be EU-listed.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most overstated proposition in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Did the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 repeal India's ship recycling law?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Section 324(1) repeals the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838 only. The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 is separate legislation and stands. The 2025 Act touches recycling only at s.17, on temporary registration of a vessel sought to be recycled.
retrieval_cards.why: A paper sat in the month the 2025 Act commenced invites exactly this error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the ICIHM from the Ready for Recycling Certificate.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials is held through the ship's service life, following initial and renewal surveys. The International Ready for Recycling Certificate is issued after the final survey, immediately before recycling, once Parts II and III of the inventory are completed and the ship recycling plan is in place.
retrieval_cards.why: One runs for the ship's life; the other is issued once, at the end.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a ship recycling facility hold under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling issued by the competent authority, and a Ship Recycling Facility Plan covering worker safety and training, emergency preparedness and response, and management of hazardous materials, with safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot-work conditions maintained.
retrieval_cards.why: The facility obligations are half the Convention and are routinely omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the binding constraint on real compliance in India?
retrieval_cards.answer: Downstream waste treatment and disposal capacity. The Convention's obligations do not end at the yard gate, and without treatment capacity for asbestos and other hazardous waste, compliance becomes documentary rather than real - which would forfeit the reputational gain that is the main prize.
retrieval_cards.why: The sharpest point available in the evaluation limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian instruments implement the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019, enacted six years before the Convention entered into force. The maritime administration is the competent authority, authorising yards and approving ship recycling plans.
retrieval_cards.why: India legislated ahead of entry into force, which is part of the significance.
